# Captain Saul

## Overview

- **Gender:** male  <sub>[v4 c13 P6](../source/v04-c13.md#nw-v04-c13-p0006), [v4 c39 P9](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0009)</sub>
- **Status:** deceased  <sub>[v4 c39 P28](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0028)</sub>
- **Role:** Lighthouse keeper and former sea captain  <sub>[v4 c9 P23](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0023), [v4 c9 P24](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0024), [v4 c24 P35](../source/v04-c24.md#nw-v04-c24-p0035)</sub>
- **Titles:** Captain Saul  <sub>[v4 c39 P20](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0020)</sub>; Captain Garrick  <sub>[v4 c24 P33](../source/v04-c24.md#nw-v04-c24-p0033)</sub>; James Garrick  <sub>[v4 c39 P5](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0005)</sub>

## Appearance

Captain Saul is an aged mariner with an elongated arm and a rough, expressive face. He lacks physical attractiveness and mourns his plain appearance. In his final days, his cheeks drained of color, though they flushed youthfully upon seeing his published book.

_Sources: [v4 c7 P61](../source/v04-c07.md#nw-v04-c07-p0061), [v4 c9 P5](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0005), [v4 c9 P6](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0006), [v4 c24 P30](../source/v04-c24.md#nw-v04-c24-p0030), [v4 c39 P4](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0004), [v4 c39 P6](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0006)_

## Personality

Captain Saul is a joyful, hospitable, and constantly good-humored individual who takes profound interior delight in every beautiful sight and sound. He possesses an unshakeable optimism and a habit of enjoying even unpleasant circumstances. Known for his keen storytelling ability, humor, and strong principles, he refuses to tolerate disparaging remarks about women. He takes intense pride in his duty, taking meticulous care to light and extinguish the lighthouse exactly at sunset and sunrise.

_Sources: [v4 c7 P63](../source/v04-c07.md#nw-v04-c07-p0063), [v4 c9 P5](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0005), [v4 c13 P15](../source/v04-c13.md#nw-v04-c13-p0015), [v4 c17 P17](../source/v04-c17.md#nw-v04-c17-p0017), [v4 c17 P18](../source/v04-c17.md#nw-v04-c17-p0018), [v4 c17 P21](../source/v04-c17.md#nw-v04-c17-p0021), [v4 c39 P16](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0016)_

## History

Captain Saul served as the keeper of the Seven Gulls lighthouse, residing at the Point with his cat, First Mate. He maintained a close friendship with Nell and Hugh Carrow, frequently welcoming them to the lighthouse or visiting their home. In an aged leather-bound volume, he penned a journal of his sea voyages and exploits—termed his "life-book"—intending to leave it to his nephew, Little Joe. Upon inspecting the text, Nell realized its narrative potential and shared it with Adrian Treleaven, who co-authored a published edition titled The Life-Book of Captain Saul. When Nell and Lorna delivered the printed volume to him, he received it with intense joy and hosted them for tea. Later that night, while reading his published life story by lamp light, Captain Saul passed away peacefully on his couch, leaving the lighthouse lit past dawn.

## Background by volume

- experienced a frightening night outdoors as an eight-year-old child before finding comfort in the moon  <sub>[v4 c7 P63](../source/v04-c07.md#nw-v04-c07-p0063)</sub>
- led an adventurous life at sea, surviving ship fires, mutinies, collisions, and encounters with Malay pirates  <sub>[v4 c24 P30](../source/v04-c24.md#nw-v04-c24-p0030)</sub>
- located Rufus Vane in Cuby and brought him back home  <sub>[v4 c13 P15](../source/v04-c13.md#nw-v04-c13-p0015)</sub>
- pruned the Lombardy trees for Miss Elizabeth  <sub>[v4 c7 P61](../source/v04-c07.md#nw-v04-c07-p0061)</sub>

## Quotes

> Mistress Carrow, I am not one for formal manners. Visiting this place brings me genuine joy, and I refuse to deprive myself simply on account of your not coming downstairs to meet me.  <sub>[v4 c9 P1](../source/v04-c09.md#nw-v04-c09-p0001)</sub>

> I’ve sort of acquired a pattern of enj’ying things. It’s become so persistent that I think I even enj’y the unpleasant things.  <sub>[v4 c17 P18](../source/v04-c17.md#nw-v04-c17-p0018)</sub>

> Knowing when to stop is something a writing woman never manages; there lies the issue. Knowing when to stop is the p’int of good writing.  <sub>[v4 c24 P28](../source/v04-c24.md#nw-v04-c24-p0028)</sub>

> Merely consider it, that aged mariner situated right in an actual published volume. Today is the most triumphant day I have ever experienced.  <sub>[v4 c39 P6](../source/v04-c39.md#nw-v04-c39-p0006)</sub>
